# Discussion
This report reflects an effort to incorporate the best available Canadian recreational catch data into the current domestic and bilateral Chinook salmon stock assessment processes. We describe methods to produce standardized post-season recreational Chinook catch estimates from 2005 to present by integrating the Internet Recreational Effort and Catch (iREC) survey with the creel and logbook programs. The updated recreational catch estimates are more spatially and temporally complete and are better aligned with an independent data set from the salmon head recovery program, than previous estimates. This report recognizes decades of improvements to catch estimation methods and applying and building upon these standardized methods in future years will allow us to continue to maintain and improve catch estimates time series over time.

The revised estimates are broadly higher for both kept and released catch than previously reported, as the updated methods are more spatially and temporally complete than previous methods. The kept catch contributed to CWT estimates that were also generally increased across fisheries and more consistent through time. Overall, the revised released catch estimates caused higher revised release rates than previously reported.  Released catch increased more in the revisions than kept catch. Released catch in general (for both creel and iREC) is more uncertain than the kept catch, primarily due to fisher recall (it's easier to recall the fish that you took home than the fish you released). Consequently, creel and logbook programs historically have poorly captured release information, although recent direction from the Selective Fisheries Evaluation Committee (SFEC) has requested more detailed release information to support the analysis of mark selective fisheries. Furthermore, unlike kept catch and the sport head recovery program, there is no (and can not be) independent verification of the enumeration of released catch (although see [@Rechinsky2025] for verification of the composition of released catch). However, release rates have been relatively stable through time, until the recent introduction of mark selective fishing and Chinook non-retention in some fisheries. This provides reassurance of release estimate precision and fisher recall, large year to year variability without regulatory changes would indicate a high degree of uncertainty in estimation. Finally,  calibration of iREC to filtered creel estimates in recent years is approaching 1:1 in a given month and area for both kept and released estimates, indicating that estimates from these independent methods are converging and providing confidence in the accuracy of all current estimation methods (see Appendix \@ref(app:apdx-irec-mthd) for more details). It is important to note that while estimates from each method are converging, the iREC survey can not be employed independently of the creel survey as it relies on creel for calibration and ground-truthing. Both the iREC estimates and the quality control criteria can be used to direct our creel survey effort in the future. 

The revised estimates varied in magnitude when compared to previous estimates between fisheries, primarily driven by differences in data quality. For example, Haida Gwaii Sport had the lowest percent change in kept catch between revised and previous estimates and there was excellent alignment with the independent sport head recovery data set using both sets of estimates and submission rates were the highest of any fishery. This indicates both accurate creel estimation by the Haida Gwaii creel survey and high participation from fishers and guides in the sport head recovery program. Central BC sport in contrast only uses logbooks (not a creel program) to estimate catch. The logbooks are also not a complete accounting of all lodges and historically an expansion factor was not applied to increase estimated catch. Consequently, the revised iREC estimates increased catch by some of the largest percentages and substantially improved alignment with sport head recoveries. iREC has therefore been incorporated into the CWT estimates for this fishery since 2019. A creel program has recently been implemented in Central BC (Area 10 beginning in 2023) and will be integrated with iREC in the future. 

Straight of Georgia Sport is another fishery with large magnitude changes from previous estimates. The quality of southern Straight of Georgia creel in particular has varied over the time series the rate of passing the criteria has gone from `r fmt_stat(all_summary_2005_2020b$pct[all_summary_2005_2020b$criteria == "passed"& all_summary_2005_2020b$region== "SGS"])`% (from 2005-2020) to `r fmt_stat(all_summary_2021_2025b$pct[all_summary_2021_2025b$criteria == "passed" & all_summary_2021_2025b$region== "SGS"])`% in the last five years (2021-2025). While improvements have been made, many factors still exist that make creel surveying in this area challenging, namely that aerial surveys must cover complex geography and dockside interviews are hindered by large numbers of launching sites, making capturing an appropriate proportion of fishers a challenge. iREC is well positioned to support the creel catch estimates in this region and consequently has been incorporated in all reporting on this fishery since 2018 (data updated back to 2013). The revised changes for this fishery between 2005 and 2012 are more aligned with recent catch and catch changes over time are less pronounced than previously reported. Further, in Southern Strait of Georgia, combined iREC and creel is more aligned with sport head recovery data than creel, particularly in the spring and fall, and this change calculates lower submission rates for this region than previously estimated. Increasing submission rates in this and other regions should help reduce uncertainty in CWT estimates. 

Within any given fishery, the quality of data underlying the revised estimates over the time series can vary widely. Higher iREC sample rates of recreational licence holders provide higher precision catch estimates in recent years, while the lack of iREC prior to 2013 and lower sample rates early in the monitoring program lead to lower confidence in earlier years. The primary reason to extend the time series back to 2005 was to provide consistent estimates for the CTC CYER base period (i.e. 2009 to 2015) and the earlier years of the associated cohorts. Future fishery assessment metrics should focus on more recent years (e.g. since the start of iREC) to reduce potential bias and imprecision when assessing recreational fisheries.

While the modelling necessarily introduced uncertainty into the estimates, the modelled estimates represent a more complete accounting (reflective of the iREC incorporation of more months and areas than creel) than previous estimates. Certainly, it provides a common currency across the CYER base period and into the future. Furthermore, the modelled estimates align between with sport head recoveries than previous estimates. The largest changes to reported estimates occur in the modelled period, mostly because updated methodology has been variably applied in recent years. There was a stronger correlation between creel summer estimates and combined creel and iREC summer estimates in the summer models compared to the correlation between creel summer estimates and combined creel and iREC spring and fall estimates in the seasonal models and between logbook or creel summer estimates and iREC estimates in the annual models. Indeed, all the summer models retained ($C_{creel,summer}$) as a variable, whereas the seasonal models for WCVI and Johnstone Strait dropped this variable as a predictor and were better described without it. This flat relationship for some seasonal fisheries explains minimal variation in the data but can give us a reasonable offset (intercept) to which we can use as a predictor for off-season catch. The previous method was to assume zero catch in the spring and fall months in these regions and therefore we see this as an improvement over previous work. While catch prediction in these regions and months could be improved with further investigation, the comparatively low number of fish caught and therefore predicted may not warrant extensive further research. 

When fitting the models between iREC and other catch monitoring programs (i.e. creel and logbooks) to infill catch estimates for pre-iREC years, most of the model fits were better as non-linear relationships. This is potentially related to the quality control filtering process of creel estimates. As effort increases in a given area and month, it likely also increases in adjoining areas and months, resulting in more area and months being included in the regional model fit. However, this may not be the case when catch monitoring program access to fishers is less of a concern. For example, a logbook program may be able to access fishers at lower efforts and provide an estimate when a creel survey may be less likely to encounter and interview fishers. This is potentially the case in the Haida Gwaii region (NBC AABM), where much of the effort is carried out by lodges that commonly participate in logbook programs. In that case, the logbook catch may have a more linear relationship with iREC catch as the bias is more evenly distributed throughout the much shorter, focused summer fishing season. The non-linearity of relationships between traditional surveys and iREC may also result from the difference in scale among the surveys and higher variability when catch estimates are high. Future efforts should aim to refine these relationships and quantify the causes of their non-linearity. 

Based on our work to date, when considering how to enhance the overall quality of recreational catch estimates in future years, we recommend focusing efforts on improving how existing data are integrated into catch estimation methods and building upon creel and iREC catch monitoring programs, as discussed below.

## Potential Estimation Improvements

The complexity of recreational catch monitoring and the extensive spatial scale of the fishery warrant further exploration of how to better apply data Canada collects to estimate catch. During the development of methods described in this report, we identified several potential improvements that should be considered in future work, including: 

 * revisiting the quality review processes to improve iREC and creel data,
 * improving the iREC-creel calibration process,
 * reviewing CWT submission rate stratification and indirect catch estimation methods,
 * incorporating creel and iREC uncertainty into model fits,
 * explore approaches to estimating mark rates.
 
As described in the methods, we defined and applied standardized data quality reviews to both the creel and iREC programs. However, as the iREC program continues to be developed and refined, more nuanced data quality reviews that incorporate additional information (e.g., regulations and fisher narratives provided with survey responses) could be explored. 

In addition to improvements in the data quality reviews, the calibration between creel and iREC has been identified as a potential area for improvement. Currently, the calibration is carried out annually for each species by their mark status and disposition (i.e., kept or released) for all areas and months. This is a "one size fits all" approach applied to a diverse range of fishing communities and regulatory regimes. The propensity for anglers to respond to the survey and their potential recall bias may vary based on angler experience, their number of trips, or the regulations that apply to the periods or areas they fish. The proportion of fishers that are guided versus unguided and the relative adoption of the avid angler program may also differ among areas and months throughout the Pacific Region, in turn influencing the relationship between creel and iREC from one area and month to the next. Improvements to the calibration process could make it more sensitive to such differences across areas, months, or years, mitigating potential confounding effects and improve catch estimate quality.

Historically, the most consistent and extensive creel program has been run in Southern BC marine waters and, for this reason, it has been applied to iREC calibrations to all regions of BC. However, as previously noted, fisher communities in Central and Northern BC may have different response rates and recall biases compared to Southern BC fishers. Accordingly, the creel and iREC calibration may be improved by incorporating creel data from these regions. 

Historic catch model fits may also be improved by accounting for uncertainty in all component datasets. A key feature of the iREC calibration process is the use of the error-in-variables approach that incorporates error in both iREC and creel catch estimates. A similar approach could be applied to historic catch models, potentially improving the accuracy and reducing possible bias of model fits, resulting in more robust estimates of catch for earlier years in the time series.

In recreational fisheries, accurate mark rates are an important component to estimating sample rates of CWT fish.  As only heads of marked fish are contributed to the program, the sample rate is estimated using the estimate of marked kept catch.  As part of both the iREC and creel programs, mark rate data is collected for both kept and released catch.  The method defined in this technical report typically selects the mark rate from one of the sources.  Future improvements to the estimation methods could look at leveraging the combined mark sample data to reduce the overall uncertainty in the marked kept catch estimate, especially in areas and times with lower fishing effort. 

## Potential Catch Monitoring Improvements

A key component to these integrated recreational catch estimation methods is the operation of creel programs. The fisher-dependent nature of the iREC catch reporting can potentially bias catch estimates if it is relied upon solely.  As described above, variability in fisher behaviour and participation rates can potentially increase the imprecision and bias of iREC catch estimates. Going forward, creel programs should continue to be a key component of recreational catch monitoring to ensure the integrity of recreational catch estimates.

Through the application of creel data in the recreational catch estimation methods described in this report, we identified a number of shortcomings that may be mitigated through shifting how the program prioritizes monitoring. We excluded some past creel data from our analyses because they were too sparse to meet minimum inclusion criteria due to too few interviews or inadequate fly over coverage for each type of day (weekend or weekday).  Where operationally feasible, it would be more beneficial to focus creel sampling on a smaller set of areas and months where more data can be collected rather than covering a wider spatio-temporal extent at a much lower sampling rate. This would maximize the amount of data from the creel program, particularly in the southern portion of BC, that could be used to accurately calibrate iREC.

One key consideration for the iREC program is how effective fishers are at communicating their catch data through the iREC reporting website. Issues, such as misunderstanding the reporting requirements of the iREC survey, or recall bias ^[Systematic error in that occurs when study participants do not remember past events or experiences accurately or completely] as a result of the time lag between catch and reporting, may reduce the quality of iREC data. Currently, the primary way to address these issues is to manually review comments provided by individual fishers. This may help resolve uncertainty in data due to misinterpreting survey questions and other issues with data entry, but is time intensive and subjective. A potentially more effective approach may be to collect fisher identification information during creel interviews (e.g., iREC access keys) to cross-reference with iREC reports. The limited number of creel interviews relative to the spatio-temporal coverage of iREC responses mean this additional information is not likely to inform the calibration directly, however, such a cross-reference between creel interviews and iREC surveys may help identify potentially systemic issues in how fishers interact with the iREC website.

A particular concern with iREC responses is the potential for recall bias resulting from the time lag between when a fishing event occurs and when it is reported in an iREC survey, which may exceed 1.5 months if the fisher waits until the deadline to report fishing events for their assigned reporting month. Therefore, any reduction to this lag may improve the overall accuracy of responses. One approach is to encourage fishers to actively record all their effort, catch, releases, and other required information (e.g., species, mark status, and length) while on the water, or shortly thereafter. DFO freely provides a document template ^[https://www.pac.dfo-mpo.gc.ca/fm-gp/rec/docs/track_catch-saisie_prises-eng.pdf] that can be printed out and carried by fishers while fishing. There are instructions on the recreational license to record all retained Chinook immediately in a table provided on the licence or to an electronic copy held in a third-party mobile application linked to their National Recreational Licensing System (NRLS) account, or directly in their NRLS account. Ideally, iREC could be linked directly to (or incorporated with) NRLS accounts so that fishers could enter iREC records at the same time that they record retained catches, consolidating all reporting requirements in one location. Emails or texts could automatically be sent to licence holders upon purchase with clear instructions on both licence and iREC reporting requirements and how and where to record information, along with links to online resources.

In general, the effectiveness of iREC is contingent on fishers knowing their responsibility to report their catch when they purchase a recreational licence. One demographic group that can be particularly challenging in this regard is guided fishers. These licence holders may be less familiar with fishing regulations, reporting requirements, the area in which they fish, or the identification of species they encounter or release. One solution is for guides to facilitate their patrons' reporting. This could be accomplished through a range of actions, from a communication campaign targeting guides and the recreational fishing industry to require guide reporting on behalf of patrons. These approaches should be considered to facilitate the improve the quality of response data from the iREC program.

# Conclusion
 
The primary goal of this work has been to incorporate direct catch estimation into a systematic, standardized, and replicable approach to better represent the impacts of Canadian marine recreational fisheries on Chinook stocks. Prior to this work, multiple methods were inconsistently applied to incorporate catch data from different sources to the estimation process. Our updated methods standardize how the data are integrated into recreational CWT estimates and how inconsistencies between sampling and catch estimates are handled. These updates leverage direct measurements and systematic methods to better reflect the recreational fishery impacts on CWT indicator stocks from 2005 to present. The revised methods described in this report provide a framework for ongoing improvements to better utilize recreational catch monitoring data and inform the operation and refinement of catch monitoring programs into the future.
